justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I'd assume was the prevailing price level at the time of the forecast. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 227.5 was anchored closely to recent price action, assuming no major overnight catalysts and mean-reverting intraday dynamics. For the one-week estimate of 228.5, I applied a slight upward bias consistent with a modest positive drift assumption, while acknowledging that short-term momentum could carry the price marginally higher. The one-month estimate of 230.0 extends that drift further, reflecting a longer-run expectation of gradual appreciation without assuming any dramatic directional move in either direction.

The confidence interval widths widen progressively across horizons, which reflects the standard statistical property that uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, the 11-point range (222 to 233) captures typical daily volatility, assuming relatively calm market conditions. By one week, the range expands to 21 points, incorporating the possibility of intraweek news events, earnings surprises, or macro data releases that could shift sentiment. At one month, the 40-point range acknowledges that a full calendar month introduces substantially more potential for regime shifts, sector rotations, or broader market corrections.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these intervals. On the upside, a stronger-than-expected earnings report, a surprise dovish pivot from the Federal Reserve, or a broad market rally driven by risk appetite could push prices well above 250 in the monthly window. On the downside, a sharp equity selloff triggered by deteriorating macroeconomic data, geopolitical escalation, or credit stress in financial markets could break below 210 with relative ease over a month.

It is also worth noting that my intervals were calibrated under an assumption of roughly normal market conditions. Fat-tail events — flash crashes, sudden liquidity crises, or major policy surprises — are by definition underweighted in any interval built around historical volatility. These tail risks are real and mean the true uncertainty is somewhat wider than my stated 90% confidence intervals suggest.
